pageCache.pageTitle: Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School and Nursery - History of Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School
pageCache.text:
History of Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School
Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School has a rich history tied to the 19th-century growth of the Catholic community in North London.
19th-Century Foundations (1870s)
Parish Origins: Sacred Heart Mission was established in the Holloway area in 1870. Following the restoration of the Catholic hierarchy in England and Wales, parish schools were founded alongside new churches to educate local Catholic working-class families.
Creation of the School: By 1879, an elementary parish school attached to the Church of the Sacred Heart was formally operating. It provided affordable education, funded by small subscriptions and parish collections.
Early 20th Century & Growth
Voluntary Aided Status: Following the Balfour Education Act of 1902 and the handover of London schools to the London County Council (LCC) in 1904, Catholic voluntary schools like Sacred Heart became part of the state-supported system while retaining their Catholic governance.
Parish Expansion: The nearby Church of the Sacred Heart on Eden Grove was formally consecrated in May 1928, establishing deep roots for the school community alongside the parish.
World War II: Like many North London schools, Sacred Heart experienced disruptions during the Blitz, including temporary pupil evacuations to rural areas outside London.
Expansion and Modern Two-Site Campus
Georges Road Base: The main primary school premises established their permanent presence at Georges Road, Holloway.
2015 Extension: To accommodate growing demand in Islington, the school expanded to operate across two sites. In 2015, a new facility at the nearby St Margaret Mary site opened to house Year 5 and Year 6 pupils. The main Georges Road building continues to serve Early Years, Key Stage 1, and lower Key Stage 2. The annexe is named after St. Margaret Mary Alacoque, the 17th-century French Roman Catholic nun and mystic whose visions established the devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus—tying the facility directly to the Catholic heritage and ethos of the school and parish. The school and church share the community centre.
Today, Sacred Heart operates as a Voluntary Aided primary school within the Diocese of Westminster and Islington Local Authority

pageCache.text:
British Values at Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School
Department for Education guidance requires schools to actively promote fundamental British Values as part of ensuring pupils are prepared for life in modern Britain.
At Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School, we fully embrace this responsibility. We are committed to promoting the fundamental British Values of:
In line with guidance from the Diocese of Westminster, we recognise that these values are not separate from our Catholic identity; rather, they are deeply rooted in the Gospel and in Catholic Social Teaching. Our mission is to place Christ at the centre of all we do, forming pupils who grow spiritually, morally, socially and culturally, so they are well prepared to take their place in modern British society and contribute to the common good.
How We Promote British Values
Democracy We teach that every person is valued and has a voice. Through the school council, pupil leadership roles and class discussions, pupils learn to participate responsibly in decision-making and to work for the good of others. This reflects the principle of participation within Catholic Social Teaching.
The Rule of Law We emphasise that laws and rules exist to ensure fairness, justice and protection for all. Pupils develop an understanding of the importance of rules in school and society, alongside their moral responsibility to act with integrity, linking to our understanding of God’s law and the call to live justly.
Individual Liberty We support pupils to develop independence and make positive choices within a safe and supportive environment. We help children to form their conscience, encouraging them to reflect on their actions and to choose what is right and loving.
Mutual Respect Rooted in the belief that all are created in the image and likeness of God, we promote dignity, kindness and forgiveness. Our community strives to follow Christ’s example by loving our neighbour and valuing each individual.
Tolerance of Different Faiths and Beliefs As part of our diverse Islington community, we promote respect for people of all faiths and none. Through our curriculum and wider experiences, pupils learn to understand and appreciate differences, recognising the right of each person to live their beliefs freely.
Catholic Distinctiveness
As a Catholic school, our promotion of British Values is enriched by Catholic Social Teaching, which provides a moral framework for living out these values. Key principles include:
Community and Participation
Solidarity and Peace
These principles are embedded across our curriculum and wider school life, including through Religious Education, PSHE, SMSC development and our wider creative curriculum. Pupils learn about democracy, civic responsibility, rules and laws, equality, environmental stewardship and respect for other faiths, making meaningful links between their own lives and those of others locally, nationally and globally.
Preparing Children for Life in Modern Britain
Promoting British Values is integral to our Catholic mission. By embedding these alongside Gospel values, we nurture pupils who are:
Through this approach, we prepare our pupils to become active, compassionate citizens who contribute positively to society and live out the values of Christ in the modern world.
Catholic Education Service Statement
Sacred Heart is a Catholic school which seeks to live out the values of Jesus Christ. We promote these values by our words and deeds, and Catholic doctrine and practice permeate every aspect of the school’s life. We provide a broad and balanced curriculum recognising that every pupil is unique and created in the image of God (Gen 1:27). Our curriculum enables each pupil to discern their vocation and to be well-equipped as active citizens in service of the world. We incorporate democratic principles, value the rule of law, support individual liberty and foster a community in which different faiths and beliefs are respected.

Our 3-5-7 Vision and Values
What is 3-5-7
Our vision for learning is brought to life through our unique 3-5-7 approach:
The "3" – Our School Rules: Ready, Respectful, Safe.
The "5" – Our Five Keys: Hunger to Achieve, Curiosity and Wonder, Community Unity, The Power of Me, and Being Safe and Responsible.
The "7" – The Learning Ladder: A structured pathway that helps pupils understand how to progress in their learning, recognizing effort, growth, and achievement at every step.

pageCache.text:
RJED (Racial Justice, Equality and Diversity)
At Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School, we are committed to promoting Racial Justice, Equality and Diversity (RJED) across all aspects of learning. Our subject leaders seek opportunities to make meaningful links to RJED with their planning, helping pupils understand its relevance through our curriculum.
In RE lessons, pupils explore different depictions of Jesus, Mary, and other religious figures from around the world, as well as a variety of religious festivals. They also experience workshops led by people of other faiths in line with Branch 6 of the RE curriculum. Focus texts in English further support pupils in understanding and celebrating cultural diversity. In Science, pupils have learnt about a wide range of scientists from diverse backgrounds and we will continue to review our curriculum this academic year to ensure that diverse backgrounds are represented in each subject.
Through these opportunities, children develop empathy, respect and an appreciation for different perspectives, helping them grow as socially aware, inclusive and thoughtful members of society.

pageCache.pageTitle: Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School and Nursery - Catholic Social Teaching
pageCache.text:
Catholic Social Teaching
Catholic Social Teaching is an approach developed by the Catholic Church on matters of social justice. It emphasises principles such as human dignity, solidarity, community, peace and the common good. The teachings aim to guide our children and institutions in creating a just and compassionate society, addressing issues like poverty, inequality, and human rights, while promoting the well-being of all members of our local and global community.
At Sacred Heart, we define Catholic Social Teaching as 'Faith in action.' It is living out our beliefs through acting for others because we believe that this is what Jesus would do and we see many examples of this in scripture.
Each half term, we focus on a different aspect of Catholic Social Teaching following the 'Caritas: Rooted in Love' planning.
Autumn 1 - Care for Creation
Autumn 2 - Preferential Option for the Poor
Spring 1 - Solidarity and Peace
Spring 2 - Community and Participation
Summer 1 - Dignity of Workers
As well as this, each year group has responsibility for one area. Each term, they complete an 'action focus' linked to their area of Catholic Social Teaching. By the time the children leave us in Year 6, they will have studied all six strands in depth and carried out many actions for others.
EYFS and Year 1 - Care for Creation
Year 2 - Preferential Option for the Poor
Year 3 - Community and Participation
Year 4 - Solidarity and Peace

pageCache.pageTitle: Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School and Nursery - Catholic Life and Mission
pageCache.text:
Catholic Life and Mission
At Sacred Heart, our Catholic faith is lived out each day through our words, actions and relationships. Our mission statement - 'To go forwards together in Christ, to respect our neighbour and to always give our best' - is at the heart of all we do at Sacred Heart. Together with parents and parish, we seek to develop and nurture the Catholic faith of our children and bring them to a fuller understanding and knowledge of Catholic teaching and tradition. The vital partnership of home, school and parish provides the context for the lifelong process of religious formation. At Sacred Heart we recognise the importance of parents as the child's first teacher and their role in faith development. We aim to work in partnership with parents and seek ways in involving them in the religious life of their children by providing opportunities for them to engage in school life. Parents are invited to attend class assemblies, whole school and class Masses. They are kept informed of what their child will be learning in Religious Education lessons and the events taking place in school through weekly newsletters and half termly Religious Education newsletters.
At Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School, children are taught the principles of Catholic Social Teaching found at the core of the Gospel.
Rooted in Love - Caritas Westminster
We use the Caritas resources and planning overview and look for opportunities to live out the principles in our faith throughout the school year.
You can find out more about this on our Catholic Social Teaching Page by clicking the image above.

pageCache.pageTitle: Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School and Nursery - Our Class Saints
pageCache.text:
Our Class Saints
There are sixteen classes in Sacred Heart ranging from Nursery to Year 6. All classes are named after a special saint. The children learn about these saints at the beginning of the year and they celebrate their feast days in school when a member of the Leadership Team leads a special prayer session and there is a celebration with cake!
Nursery - St Anthony of Padua
Feast Day: 13th June
Patron Saint of: Lost items, lost people, and helpfulness
Saint Anthony was a kind and humble Franciscan friar who dedicated his life to preaching God's word, helping the poor, and sharing God's love with everyone he met.
He is best known around the world as the patron saint of lost things. A well-known story tells of a lost book of Psalms that was returned after Saint Anthony prayed for it. Today, Christians ask Saint Anthony to pray for them when they misplace an item, but more importantly, to help find things that matter most—like peace, kindness, and faith when they feel lost.
Nursery - St Nicholas
Feast Day: 6th December
Patron Saint of: Children, sailors, and secret gift-giving
Saint Nicholas was a kindly Christian bishop who lived in Myra (in modern-day Turkey) many hundreds of years ago. He is remembered today as a model of generosity, care for children, and compassion for anyone in need.
He is most famous for his secret acts of kindness. In one well-known story, he helped a poor family by secretly tossing three bags of gold coins through their window at night, ensuring they had enough money to live peacefully. His reputation for giving gifts in secret inspired the tradition of Santa Claus around Christmas time!
Reception - St Peter
Feast Day: 29th June
Patron Saint of: The Church, fishermen, and popes
Saint Peter was a fisherman named Simon who became one of Jesus' very first disciples and closest friends. Jesus gave him the name Peter, which means "Rock," and chose him to be the leader of the Apostles and the very first Pope.
Although Peter was brave, he was also human and made mistakes—like losing faith in the storm or denying he knew Jesus three times. However, Peter always asked for forgiveness and showed deep love for God. His story reminds us that God doesn't expect us to be perfect, but calls us to be faithful, forgiving, and strong in our love for others.
Feast Day: 28th October
Patron Saint of: Hope, difficult situations, and lost causes
Saint Jude (also known as Thaddeus) was one of Jesus’ twelve original disciples and a close companion during His ministry. After the Resurrection, Saint Jude traveled far and wide to spread the Good News, teaching people about God's love and encouraging them to stay strong in their faith during tough times.
He is loved around the world as the patron saint of hope. Whenever people face tricky problems, feel worried, or think something is impossible, they pray to Saint Jude to remind them that with God, there is always hope and a way forward.
Feast Day: 1st February
Patron Saint of: Ireland, nature, newborns, and hospitality
Saint Brigid is one of the most famous saints of Ireland, living in the 5th century. She was known for her immense generosity, her deep love for God's creation, and her devotion to helping the poor, the sick, and travellers. She founded a famous monastery in Kildare that welcomed anyone in need of food, shelter, or prayer.
According to a well-known story, when a local chieftain refused to give her land to build a monastery for the poor, Brigid asked for only as much land as her cloak could cover. When she spread her cloak on the ground, it miraculously stretched out in all directions to cover acres of green fields!
Year 1 - St Francis of Assisi
Feast Day: 4th October
Patron Saint of: Animals, nature, ecology, and peacemakers
Saint Francis was born into a wealthy family in Italy, but he gave up all his money, fine clothes, and earthly possessions to live a simple life following Jesus. He dedicated himself to serving the poor, spreading peace, and praising God for the beauty of the natural world.
Saint Francis believed that every part of creation was a gift from God. He referred to the sun, moon, wind, and stars as his brothers and sisters! Legends say that animals loved his gentle presence—he famously preached sermons to flocks of birds and made peace with a dangerous wolf that was scaring a local village.
Year 2 - St Teresa of Calcutta
Feast Day: 5th September
Patron Saint of: World Youth Day, practical help, and charitable causes
Saint Teresa of Calcutta (often known as Mother Teresa) was a Catholic nun who spent her life helping poor, sick, and lonely people.
Born in 1910, she moved to India as a young woman and worked as a teacher. Seeing so many people in need, she decided to live among the poorest families in Calcutta, establishing schools, medical clinics, and homes for the homeless. She founded the Missionaries of Charity to spread love and care across the globe, earning the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.
Her message for young people was simple: "Not all of us can do great things. But we can do small things with great love." She teaches us that every small act of kindness—from a helpful hand to a simple smile—makes the world a brighter place.
Year 2 - St John Paul
Feast Day: 22nd October
Patron Saint of: World Youth Day, young people, and families
Saint John Paul II was a beloved leader of the Catholic Church who served as Pope for nearly 27 years, sharing God’s message of love, peace, and hope all across the globe.
Born in Poland in 1920, he loved playing football, skiing, and acting in plays as a boy. As a young man, he lived through hard times during World War II, but his strong faith guided him to become a priest and later the Pope in 1978. He became one of the most traveled world leaders in history, visiting over 100 countries to meet people of all faiths and cultures.
Saint John Paul II had a special place in his heart for young people and created World Youth Day to bring children and teenagers together from around the world. He famously reminded everyone, "Do not be afraid!" and showed incredible forgiveness by visiting and forgiving the man who once tried to hurt him. He teaches us to be brave, love others unconditionally, and stand up for peace.
Year 3 - St Martin De Porres
Feast Day: 3rd November
Patron Saint of: Social justice, barbers, public health workers, and racial harmony
Saint Martin de Porres was a kind and humble Dominican brother in Peru who spent his entire life caring for those in need, regardless of who they were.
Born in Lima, Peru, in 1579, Martin grew up poor and faced unkindness because of his mixed heritage. Instead of feeling bitter, he chose to fill his heart with God's love. He trained as a medical worker and barber, using his skills to heal the sick, feed hundreds of hungry people every day, and establish a shelter for homeless children.
He was happy to do even the simplest chores - he teaches us that humility, kindness, and treating everyone equally can change the world.
Year 3 - St Bernadette
Feast Day: 16th April
Patron Saint of: Illness, poor people, shepherds, and Lourdes
Saint Bernadette was a humble young girl from France whose courage, honesty, and deep faith inspired millions of people around the world.
Born in Lourdes in 1844, Bernadette grew up in a very poor family and suffered from ill health throughout her life. In 1858, when she was just 14 years old, Mary, the Mother of Jesus, appeared to her in a cave called a grotto. Mary asked Bernadette to dig in the dirt, uncovering a natural spring of fresh water that still flows today and has brought healing to many sick people.
Even when some adults didn't believe her story at first, Bernadette remained gentle, truthful, and brave. She later became a nun, spending her days quietly praying and caring for others. She teaches us that God chooses ordinary, gentle people to do extraordinary things, and that staying truthful and faithful gives us strength.
Year 4 - St Catherine of Alexandria
Feast Day: 25th November
Patron Saint of: Students, teachers, librarians, philosophers, and scholars
Saint Catherine of Alexandria was a clever and brave princess from Egypt who loved learning and used her wisdom to stand up for her faith. Born in the city of Alexandria around 287 AD, Catherine studied hard from a young age and became famous for her incredible intelligence. When an Emperor began treating Christians unfairly, 18-year-old Catherine bravely spoke to him and explained why believing in God was important. The Emperor called fifty of his top scholars to debate with her, but Catherine spoke with such wisdom and kindness that many of them were inspired by her words.
Year 4 - St Elizabeth of Hungary
Feast Day: 17th November
Patron Saint of: Hospitals, nurses, bakers, homeless people, and charities
Saint Elizabeth of Hungary was a generous princess who chose to use her royal wealth and power to care for poor, hungry, and sick people.
Born in Hungary in 1207, Elizabeth grew up living in a royal castle in Germany. Even though she was a princess, she wore simple clothes and spent her days helping those in need. She built a hospital near her home and personally cared for the sick, serving them food and giving them fresh clothing.
Famous stories tell of the "Miracle of the Roses": while carrying loaves of bread hidden under her cloak to feed poor families, she was asked what she was holding, and when she opened her mantle, the bread had turned into a bunch of beautiful red and white roses! Saint Elizabeth teaches us that sharing what we have with kindness and generosity is one of the greatest ways to show God's love.
Year 5 - St Faustina Kowalski
Feast Day: 5th October
Patron Saint of: Mercy, forgiveness, and World Youth Day
Saint Faustina Kowalska was a gentle Polish nun who shared a special message with the world about God’s infinite love, kindness, and forgiveness.
Born in Poland in 1905, Helena grew up in a large, hardworking family. From a young age, she loved praying and helping others, and as a young woman she joined the convent, taking the name Sister Faustina. She spent her days working quietly as a cook, gardener, and door keeper, doing everyday tasks with a cheerful heart.
During her life, Faustina had visions of Jesus, who asked her to remind everyone that God's love is endless. She worked with an artist to paint the famous Divine Mercy image, showing Jesus with red and pale rays of light coming from His heart to bless the world. Saint Faustina wrote a personal diary full of prayers, teaching us that no matter what mistakes we make, we can always say, "Jesus, I trust in You," and share His mercy with others.
Year 5 - St Benedict the Moor
Feast Day: 4th April
Patron Saint of: African Americans, kitchen workers, cooks, and Palermo
Saint Benedict the Moor was a humble Franciscan friar who became famous for his wisdom, deep faith, and gentle kindness toward everyone he met.
Born near Messina, Sicily, in 1526, Benedict's parents had been brought from Africa to Italy. Though he grew up poor and was never taught to read or write, Benedict loved God deeply and joined a community of Franciscans as a young man. He worked for many years in the monastery kitchen, happily preparing meals for his fellow friars and visitors.
Even though he held simple jobs, people from all around came to Benedict for advice because of his incredible patience, understanding, and wise words. He was eventually chosen to lead his monastery, guiding others with great humility and love. Saint Benedict the Moor teaches us that you don't need fancy titles or high education to be wise, and that serving others with a cheerful heart is a true gift from God.
Year 6 - St Maximilian Kolbe
Feast Day: 14th August
Patron Saint of: Families, journalists, prisoners, and the pro-life movement
Saint Maximilian Kolbe was a heroic Polish priest who showed the ultimate power of love and sacrifice by putting others before himself.
Born in Poland in 1894, Maximilian loved science, invention, and serving God from a young age. As a priest, he used modern technology to share God’s love, creating a special magazine and running a radio station. He even traveled as a missionary to Japan, building a monastery near Nagasaki.
During World War II, Father Kolbe helped protect thousands of refugees in Poland. When he was later imprisoned in a concentration camp, he kept up the spirits of those around him by praying, singing hymns, and sharing his food. When a fellow prisoner with a family was chosen to be punished, Father Kolbe bravely stepped forward and volunteered to take his place, saving the man's life. He famously said, "Hatred is not a creative force: only love is creative." Saint Maximilian Kolbe teaches us the beauty of selflessness and how true love means caring for others even when it is difficult.
Year 6 - St Josephine Bakhita
Feast Day: 8th February
Patron Saint of: Victims of modern slavery, human trafficking, and Sudan
Saint Josephine Bakhita was a gentle and forgiving religious sister from Sudan who showed that love, hope, and faith can overcome even the hardest times.
Born in Darfur, Sudan, around 1869, Josephine was kidnapped as a child and sold into slavery, where she was treated very harshly and given the name "Bakhita," which means "fortunate." Eventually, a kind Italian family brought her to Italy, where she learned about God for the very first time. When she gained her freedom, she chose to become a Catholic nun with the Canossian Sisters.
Sister Josephine spent over forty years in Italy working as a cook, seamstress, and doorkeeper. Children loved her warm smile, sweet voice, and comforting presence. She never held anger in her heart for those who had hurt her in the past, famously saying, "If I were to meet the slave-traders who kidnapped me... I would kneel and kiss their hands, for if that had not happened, I would not be a Christian today." Saint Josephine Bakhita teaches us the power of forgiveness, the dignity of ev

Our Parish
Our Parish
Sacred Heart School is happy to work in partnership with the parish community of Sacred Heart church.
Parish website: sacred heart church holloway
Read about the history of our parish church here: Parish History – sacred heart church holloway
Children attend Mass on Holy Days of Obligation that fall in term time, at the beginning of each term, other special occasions and on Sacred Heart feast day. Children from Y3 –Y6 also attend the Wednesday parish mass on a rota basis and Years 1 and 2 celebrate a liturgy in school with Father Francis. During other times of the liturgical year children visit the church for Stations of the Cross, the Sacrament of Reconciliation and Eucharistic Adoration, as well as visits that link to the current RE topic.
Fr Francis, Father Spencer and Father Samuel are regular visitors to the school and lead liturgical prayer sessions for children across the school. Children take part in parish liturgies acting as altar servers and involve themselves in events organised by the parish e.g. Church Nativity Play and Stations of the Cross.

pageCache.pageTitle: Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School and Nursery - Religious Education
pageCache.text:
Religious Education
At Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School, Religious Education is at the core of our curriculum. Through the teaching of RE we will support our children to become religiously literate and engaged young people who have the knowledge, understanding and skills to reflect spiritually, and think ethically and theologically. Through the teaching of Religious Education, we instil a strong belief that we must value and respect one another and our environment for the common good.
Religious Education in the curriculum
At Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School, we are following the new Religious Education Directory (RED) from September 2025. The RED includes a ‘Model curriculum’ that staff have received significant training and support to plan high-quality and enriching learning experiences.
Teachers are encouraged to be as creative as possible in their lesson planning and to employ a range of teaching styles. The RED is scripture based, following the story of Jesus, and it is an invitation to ‘Know Him more clearly’. Teachers include teaching and connections with Prayer and Liturgy, as well as Rooted in Love, the Diocese of Westminster Catholic Social Teaching program.
The curriculum has six components that are known as branches which will be taught one per half term across the six half-terms of the school year. Each one has a core theme and invites pupils to learn about an aspect of Revelation, Scripture, life in Christ, and life in the Church, and to discern what their learning means academically and experientially enabling them to see, judge, and act through a deeper knowledge of the Christian faith.
Branch 1 – Creation and covenant: ‘The heavens are telling the glory of God’ (Ps 19:1). In this branch, pupils will encounter the God who creates and calls a people. They will explore revelation of the Christian belief that all that is comes from God, the Creation accounts in Genesis, and scientific explanations of the process of Creation. They will explore the call of God and his covenantal relationship with his people first through Abraham and Moses, then through the narrative of the Old Testament.
Branch 2 – Prophecy and promise: ‘In many and various ways, God spoke to our ancestors by the prophets’ (Heb 1:1). The prophets speak of God reaching to his people, calling them back into a relationship with him. In this branch, pupils will explore the Christian understanding of the teaching of the prophets as they point to the fulfilment of God’s promise in a messiah, Jesus Christ. They will explore the expectant waiting for the Messiah through the Advent season and how this speaks to Christians today as they wait for Christ. Pupils will encounter the story of the nativity of Jesus and the mystery of the incarnation.
Branch 3 – Galilee to Jerusalem: ‘God’s only Son, who is at the Father’s side, has made him known’ (Jn 1:18). In this branch, pupils will experience the ministry of Jesus, the Word of God. They will learn about the life of Jesus and his revelation of the Kingdom of God through parables, encounters, miracles, and teachings. They will learn about the call of the disciples and the nature of being a follower of Jesus.
Branch 4 – Desert to garden: ‘Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day’ (1 Cor 15:3). In this branch, pupils will study the season of Lent and its culmination in the events of Holy Week. They will learn about the Paschal Triduum at the heart of the Catholic Church’s Liturgy and life. The title of this branch points both to the liturgical journey from the desert of Lent to the garden of Resurrection, but also to the Paschal journey from darkness to light, barrenness to fruitfulness, death to life.
Branch 5 – To the ends of the Earth: ‘Go, therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Mt 28:19). In this branch, pupils will study the events that flowed from the Resurrection and Ascension in the coming of the Holy Spirit and the work of the apostles and early Church. They will also learn about the Catholic Church today as the apostolic Church and how its liturgy and structures flow from the early Church.
Branch 6 – Dialogue and encounter: ‘For “In him we live and move and have our being”’ (Acts 17:28). In this branch, pupils will learn how Christians work together with people of different religious convictions and all people of goodwill towards the common good, respecting the dignity of all humanity. They will also encounter other pathways of belief drawing on the teaching of the Church about intercultural dialogue.
A bit more about Branch 6…
Dialogue: What the Church teaches about the relationship between Catholicism and other Christian traditions, Judaism, Islam, other world views and non-religious word views.
Encounter: A discrete study of other faiths, religions and world views. The order that pupils learn about other world religions is based on the model provided by Pope St Paul VI in his encyclical Ecclesiam Suam.
Branch 6 is supplemented with religious workshops (Judaism, Islam and Hinduism) and religious speakers. Special dates and events, such as Diwali are focused on in assemblies and our Early Years have celebration books where they look at religious festivals when they occur.

pageCache.pageTitle: Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School and Nursery - The Sacred Heart of Jesus and St Margaret Mary Alacoque
pageCache.text:
The Sacred Heart of Jesus and St Margaret Mary Alacoque
The Sacred Heart is one of the most loved devotions in the Catholic Church. It represents:
Jesus’ unconditional love for every person
Compassion, mercy and forgiveness
A heart that is open to all, especially the vulnerable
A call to love others as Christ loves us
The image of the Sacred Heart often shows:
A heart surrounded by flames (symbolising burning love)
A crown of thorns (Christ’s suffering for humanity)
A cross rising from the heart (His sacrifice)
Light shining from the heart (His divine love)
The children created some lovely homework pieces on the Sacred Heart which are now displayed in school:
St Margaret Mary Alacoque
St Margaret Mary Alacoque (1647–1690) was a French nun who received visions of Jesus revealing His Sacred Heart. She is known for:
Her deep prayer life
Her message that Jesus’ heart burns with love for all people
Encouraging devotion to the Sacred Heart
Inspiring the tradition of First Fridays and Holy Hours
As part of our work on Sacred Heart Feast Day, we created a display about the life of St Margaret Mary Alacoque:

pageCache.pageTitle: Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School and Nursery - Welcome
pageCache.text:
Welcome
Welcome from our Executive Headteacher - Mr Lane
Welcome to Sacred Heart Catholic Primary School! We are dedicated to nurturing the academic and spiritual development of every child. Our school has a proud tradition of fostering growth and excellence, and we warmly invite families from all faiths and backgrounds to join our community.
As Catholic educators, we embed the teachings of the Gospel to inspire pupils to achieve their best. Jesus Christ is at the centre of our school life, guiding us with His example of love, kindness, and service. This shapes the way we learn, grow, and care for one another, creating a supportive and caring environment.
We are proud to be a welcoming and inclusive community where all families are valued and respected. By working in close partnership with parents and our parish, we provide every child with a strong foundation for lifelong learning, character, and faith.
Our vision for learning is brought to life through our unique 3-5-7 approach:
The "3" – Our School Rules: Ready, Respectful, Safe.
The "5" – Our Five Keys: Hunger to Achieve, Curiosity and Wonder, Community Unity, The Power of Me, and Being Safe and Responsible.
The "7" – The Learning Ladder: A structured pathway that helps pupils understand how to progress in their learning, recognizing effort, growth, and achievement at every step.
Sacred Heart is a busy, friendly two-form entry school for children aged 3 to 11, based across two sites. Our Year 5 and Year 6 classes are located at the Saint Margaret Mary Annexe, which we share with our parish Community Centre. This site also houses our well-loved school library, which all pupils regularly visit.
We are committed to keeping our families informed and involved through weekly newsletters and regular social media updates. We look forward to working closely with you and your child throughout their journey at Sacred Heart. With the dedication of our staff, the strength of our community, and the grace of our shared faith, we aim to nurture compassionate, capable children ready to make a difference in today’s world.
If you’re interested in joining our vibrant school community, please contact the school office between 8am-4pm to arrange a tour of our school.
Warm Regards, Mr John Lane Executive Head teacher
